@graph.headline: Hash, Don't Host: What Blockchain-Verified Records Store, and What Never Leaves Your Building
@graph.description: Encrypted data on a ledger is still personal data — the EDPB settled that in July 2026. Here is what a verifiable record should actually store, what should never leave your building, and why hashing is the only design that survives the regulator and the invoice.

about.name: Data placement in blockchain-verified business records — what is committed on-chain versus stored off-chain, the EDPB's July 2026 three-criteria anonymisation test, key and salt destruction as erasure proxies, on-chain storage cost physics, and HIPAA and attorney-client privilege mapping

mainEntity.name: Does anything personal ever go on the blockchain in a verifiable record?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. In a properly built verifiable workflow the chain receives fingerprints, timestamps, and pseudonymous actor identifiers — never names, patient data, or privileged content. If a vendor proposes storing the records themselves on-chain, that is the architecture to walk away from.

mainEntity.name: Is a hash of personal data still personal data?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. The EDPB's July 2026 guidelines treat hashed and encrypted on-chain data as personal data when it can be linked back to an individual. A hash of a document held in a deletable off-chain database, with no linkable external identifier, is the version that can qualify as genuinely anonymous.

mainEntity.name: How do you satisfy a deletion or amendment request if a record is on a chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two mechanisms are accepted: destroy the decryption key, or destroy the salt. Either renders the on-chain commitment unusable without altering the ledger. HIPAA's amendment right under 45 CFR 164.526 is handled the same way — correct the off-chain record, fingerprint the correction, and keep the audit trail intact.

mainEntity.name: Why not use a private blockchain and store everything there?

acceptedAnswer.text: Private and consortium chains do solve the controller-identification problem the EDPB raises, and they are the right structure when on-chain personal data is genuinely unavoidable. They do not solve cost or custody: you still pay per byte, and you still need key and salt discipline. For most businesses the simpler answer is a public chain for proofs and your own systems for content.

mainEntity.name: What does a verifiable record cost to run?

acceptedAnswer.text: The on-chain footprint is 32 bytes per record — a few cents of gas under most conditions, against roughly $1,300 per megabyte for storing actual data. The real cost is the workflow build and the key-custody process around it, which is a one-time engagement rather than a per-record meter.

mainEntity.name: What should a Metro Detroit business do before putting anything on-chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Inventory which records anyone will ever dispute, classify each field as content or proof, and confirm that no document, identifier, or privileged sentence is scheduled for a public write. That inventory takes an afternoon and tells you whether your current automation is an asset or a liability.
